explanations.explanation: Paul says it right there: the gospel is what he preached to them, what they received, and what they "stand firm" in (1 Corinthians 15:1). That's a church planted like a tree, not blowing around like flour. I think Paul is smiling a little as he writes it.

explanations.answer: They argue over every word of it
explanations.explanation: Nothing in this verse says they argue over it. Paul says they received the gospel and "stand firm" in it (1 Corinthians 15:1). Some folks would argue with a cookie recipe, but that's not what the text says about the Corinthians here.

Paul never says that. He says the gospel is what he preached to them, what they received, and where they "stand firm" (1 Corinthians 15:1). Keeping a warm batch all to yourself is a real temptation, but it isn't in this verse.

explanations.answer: Hold firmly to the word he preached
explanations.explanation: Paul says, "By this gospel you are saved, if you hold firmly to the word I preached to you." (1 Corinthians 15:2) So that little "if" points right back to the word he preached. Hold on to it, friend, like a baker holds a hot tray with two good mitts.

A trip to Jerusalem isn't what Paul puts after the "if." He says they're saved if they "hold firmly to the word I preached to you." (1 Corinthians 15:2) No plane tickets, no packing, just holding on to the word.

explanations.answer: Keep every feast in the law
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't mention feasts here at all. The "if" is about holding "firmly to the word I preached to you." (1 Corinthians 15:2) I love a good feast, but that's not the condition in this verse.

Paul says the opposite. He says that if they don't hold firmly to the word he preached, "you have believed in vain." (1 Corinthians 15:2) In vain means it comes to nothing. So their believing wouldn't count for something in that case.

Right, because Paul says that without holding firmly to the word he preached, "you have believed in vain." (1 Corinthians 15:2) So believing doesn't still count for something in that case. It's like pulling a tray out of a cold oven. You did all the stirring, and nothing came of it.

Paul says, "For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance." (1 Corinthians 15:3) He's a delivery guy here, not the inventor. He got it, and he handed it on. I know that feeling, because somebody handed me a whole new life once.
The word is "received." Paul says, "For what I received I passed on to you…" (1 Corinthians 15:3) He didn't make up this message. He got it and passed it on, so he's carrying it, not writing it.

Paul never says he changed it. He says, "For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance." (1 Corinthians 15:3) He received it and passed it on as he got it. That's a baker who follows the recipe card.

Paul says Christ "was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures." (1 Corinthians 15:4) The list goes death, burial, raised, and the burial isn't the final word. The third day is where the story turns.

Paul says the third day, not the seventh. He says Christ "was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures." (1 Corinthians 15:4) Seven days would be a long wait, friend. The text gives us three.
Forty days isn't the number Paul gives for the raising. He says Christ "was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures." (1 Corinthians 15:4) That's three days, not forty.

Yes, and Paul says it twice in a row. Christ died for our sins "according to the Scriptures," and He was raised on the third day "according to the Scriptures." (1 Corinthians 15:3-4) Same phrase for the death and for the raising. Paul wants us to see both of them together.

It's true, though. Paul says Christ died for our sins "according to the Scriptures," and then says He was raised on the third day "according to the Scriptures." (1 Corinthians 15:3-4) The phrase shows up for both the death and the raising. Count them, friend, there are two.
Paul says Christ "appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve." (1 Corinthians 15:5) The Twelve are the group of disciples Jesus chose to follow Him. So Peter sees Him, and then the whole group does.

The Pharisees aren't on Paul's list here. He says Christ "appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve." (1 Corinthians 15:5) The Twelve are the disciples Jesus chose to follow Him. Paul is naming those who saw Him.
Not the chief priests. Paul says Christ "appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve." (1 Corinthians 15:5) The Twelve are the disciples Jesus chose to follow Him. That's the next name on the list.

Paul says Christ "appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once." (1 Corinthians 15:6) Five hundred! That's a bigger crowd than any bakery line I've ever seen. And they all saw Him at the same time.
That number isn't in this verse. Paul says Christ "appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once." (1 Corinthians 15:6) Five hundred is a way bigger crowd than a hundred twenty, friend.

Paul doesn't give an exact small number like that. He says Christ "appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once." (1 Corinthians 15:6) Five hundred and then some. That's a whole lot of witnesses.

Paul says the opposite. He says that of the more than five hundred, "most of whom are still living, though some have fallen asleep." (1 Corinthians 15:6) Most are still living, and only some have fallen asleep. That means you could still go ask them.

Right on. Paul says the more than five hundred are "most of whom are still living, though some have fallen asleep." (1 Corinthians 15:6) So most are still alive when he writes. I think Paul is saying you can go ask them yourself.
Paul says, "And last of all He appeared to me also." (1 Corinthians 15:8) He puts himself at the very end of the list. The man holding the pen is the last name on it.

It's true, friend. Paul says, "And last of all He appeared to me also, as to one of untimely birth." (1 Corinthians 15:8) He's the one writing the letter, and he puts himself at the very end of the list.

explanations.answer: He persecuted the church of God
explanations.explanation: Paul says he's unworthy "because I persecuted the church of God." (1 Corinthians 15:9) He doesn't hide it or dress it up. He says it plain, and I respect that.

explanations.answer: He was the youngest of them
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't give his age as the reason. He says he's unworthy "because I persecuted the church of God." (1 Corinthians 15:9) That's the reason in the text, and nothing about being youngest.
Paul doesn't say that here. His reason is, "because I persecuted the church of God." (1 Corinthians 15:9) The text points to his past, not to a missing miracle.
Paul says, "But by the grace of God I am what I am." (1 Corinthians 15:10) He gives God the credit. The least of the apostles didn't climb up there, he was given a hand.
Paul doesn't credit his studying here. He says, "But by the grace of God I am what I am." (1 Corinthians 15:10) The credit goes to God's grace, not to a pile of books.
Paul doesn't point to the apostles' approval. He says, "But by the grace of God I am what I am." (1 Corinthians 15:10) He gives the credit to God's grace, and he doesn't hand out a vote.

Paul says, "I worked harder than all of them." (1 Corinthians 15:10) Then he quickly adds, "yet not I, but the grace of God that was with me." So he names his hard work and hands the credit right back to God's grace.

It's true, friend. Paul says, "No, I worked harder than all of them." (1 Corinthians 15:10) And then he adds, "yet not I, but the grace of God that was with me." He says it and he gives God the credit in the same breath.

Paul says, "Whether, then, it was I or they, this is what we preach, and this is what you believed." (1 Corinthians 15:11) Paul and the other apostles all preach the same message. And the Corinthians believed it, which is good news for them.

The word is "preach," not "question." Paul says, "this is what we preach, and this is what you believed." (1 Corinthians 15:11) The apostles all preach the same thing, and Paul doesn't say a word about questioning it.
Nice try, but the word is "preach." Paul says, "this is what we preach, and this is what you believed." (1 Corinthians 15:11) Singing is great, friend, and I'd hum along. But Paul says preach.
